title: Reverie Moments
tagline: Twelve contradictions found in a scope of work, before a line of it was built.
summary: A discovery audit of the scope of work for a group-and-crew travel operations platform, and the role research the document was missing.
timeline: PLACEHOLDER — engagement dates pending. Ran as phases 2 to 5 of a structured discovery session.

about: Reverie Moments runs group and crew travel services — programs made of individual services, each assigned to vendors, drivers and Guest Ambassadors, and executed to the minute on the day. Today that entire operation runs on paper and Excel; there is no digital system at all, which the scope of work names directly as the inefficiency the platform exists to remove. I was brought in against the SOW itself, at version 0.1, to audit what it specified before it was built, and to write the role research it was missing. The finding that shaped the engagement: Operations — the role that owns the platform’s two most time-critical dashboards — had no documented journey. Section 1.22, the section reserved for it, was marked work-in-progress, and its only sentence described the Sales team.

metrics.label: Contradictions and gaps documented
metrics.note: Each one traced to a specific SOW section or Phase 2 finding, with a severity and a proposed resolution.

metrics.label: High-severity, all on the Operations path
metrics.note: They shared a root cause: the OPS-facing sections were left incomplete relative to the equivalent GCSM ones.

metrics.label: Findings traced to a clause
metrics.note: Gap and friction analysis findings A1 through F1, each cited to the section it contradicts.

metrics.label: Requirements invented
metrics.note: Zero-assumptions policy: anything the SOW did not answer was flagged as an open question, never filled in.

research.intro: No interviews were available and no external research was permitted, so the method had to work entirely from the document and from what the client confirmed about current state. That constraint turned out to be the useful one: reading a specification against itself, clause by clause, surfaces the contradictions that only appear when two sections are asked the same question.

methods.name: Clause-by-clause read
methods.detail: Sections 1.9, 1.13, 1.19, 1.22, 1.26, 1.27, 1.30 and 1.32, read for what each one claims a role can do.

methods.name: Permission-matrix reconciliation
methods.detail: Every narrative statement about who does what, checked against the CRUD permission matrix in §1.9.

methods.name: Cross-section contradiction tracing
methods.detail: Where two sections disagreed, both were cited and the disagreement logged as a finding rather than resolved by guess.

methods.name: Current-state confirmation
methods.detail: Client context on the existing process: paper and spreadsheets, no digital system, every handoff manual.

research.insight: The role with the most operationally critical, real-time responsibilities was the one the document described least. §1.22, reserved for the Operations user flow, was marked WIP and its only text described Sales — while §1.13 and §1.27 gave OPS exclusive ownership of the Daily OPSKED and the live execution dashboard.
research.insightAttribution: Reverie Moments SOW V.0.1, §1.22 against §1.13 and §1.27

painPoints.label: The critical role has no documented journey
painPoints.detail: OPS owns publishing the Daily OPSKED and tracking live execution, yet the section meant to document how it works was a placeholder describing a different team. Every OPS stage in this engagement had to be reconstructed from adjacent sections.
painPoints.evidence: SOW §1.22 against §1.13 and §1.27 — Finding A1, high severity

painPoints.label: Billing responsibility contradicts billing access
painPoints.detail: The Billing Journey narrative states that OPS enters charges, units and client billing details. The §1.9 permission matrix grants OPS no billing access whatsoever — not create, read, update or delete.
painPoints.evidence: SOW §1.9 against the Billing Journey — Finding B1, high severity

painPoints.label: A reassignment can silently double-book a vendor
painPoints.detail: Vendor availability checking is described in the SOW but explicitly excluded from MVP scope. The moment OPS reassigns a vendor mid-disruption — exactly when it matters — nothing flags the overlap.
painPoints.evidence: Vendor Assignment to Service Cards — Finding C3, high severity

painPoints.label: Offline support with no conflict rule
painPoints.detail: Offline and local sync is named as a requirement, but no conflict-resolution behaviour is defined. OPS is the role most likely to be working in the field on poor connectivity, which puts the risk on the platform’s own real-time tracking objective.

matrix.caption: What the narrative promises, against what the §1.9 permission matrix actually grants

rows.label: Billing — OPS
values: OPS enters charges, units and client billing details
Grant matrix access to match the narrative, or restrict OPS and correct every downstream doc

rows.label: Trouble tickets — Vendor
values: Vendor has no row in the matrix
Add Vendor as a first-class role, or document that OPS enters transitions on their behalf

rows.label: Vendor availability
values: Non-blocking overlap warning on date and time collisions

rows.label: Notification triggers
values: Ticket status and driver-unavailable alerts described
Add explicit rows with sender, receiver and content

rows.label: Manifest templates
values: Full per-role CRUD still defined beneath it
Remove the rows, or mark them reserved for a later phase

rows.label: Vendor performance
values: Vendor profile shows performance metrics and feedback
Monitoring and rating are both descoped
Cut the reference, or scope one minimal performance field

competitiveAudit.whitespace: Nobody had written down how Operations actually spends its day. The Sales and Tour Desk journeys were templated from GCSM rather than authored, and the OPS section was empty — so the platform was about to be built around the one role whose workflow nobody had described. That is the gap: not a missing feature, a missing document, and everything downstream inherited it.

personas.name: Group & Crew Services Manager
personas.role: Program owner and primary client contact
personas.quote: My job is to keep every program on schedule and ready to bill — but I only see what’s been published to me, and today none of this is even digital yet.
goals: Carry every program from Active through InProgress to Operated, complete enough for Accounting to bill against.
Hold one accurate source of truth, so client-facing reports match what the team sees internally.
Coordinate vendors and internal assignments across Sales, Tour Desk and Guest Ambassadors without conflicts.
Resolve service and program issues before they reach the client relationship.
frustrations: Day-of visibility is read-only and second-hand: only as good as what OPS publishes, and how promptly.
None of it is digital yet — the coordination this platform is meant to replace happens on paper and in spreadsheets.
No safeguard against double-booking a vendor across overlapping services; availability checking is out of MVP scope.
Vendor has no row in the permission matrix, so there is no rule for what a vendor may do with a ticket assigned to them.
personas.note: A role persona, not a person. The SOW documents responsibilities and permissions, not demographics, so age, education and location are recorded as not specified rather than invented. The quote is synthesised from documented responsibilities.

personas.name: Operations
personas.role: Real-time execution owner — Daily and Live OPSKED
personas.quote: I’m the one who has to catch problems while they’re still happening in the field — but my own journey through this platform isn’t written down anywhere yet.
goals: Publish a Daily OPSKED accurate enough that every other role can plan their day against it.
Track live execution and catch delays, flight issues and tickets while they are still happening.
Reassign vendors, drivers and Guest Ambassadors quickly when a service breaks, without losing the audit trail.
Resolve or escalate trouble tickets before they reach a guest.
frustrations: The section meant to document this role’s journey is work-in-progress, and describes the Sales team instead.
Ticket status-change and driver-unavailable alerts are described in the functional sections but missing from the notification table.
No availability check exists, so a mid-disruption reassignment can silently collide with an existing commitment.
Offline support is required but undefined: no conflict rule, on the role most likely to be working without signal.
personas.note: Built entirely from the role definition in §1.13, the permission matrix in §1.9 and the OPSKED and trouble-ticket sections, because the dedicated OPS journey section contains no OPS content. Where this persona bridges two sections, it says so.

journey.label: Operations, from morning review to day-end rollover

stages.name: Daily review and prep
stages.goal: Get oriented on what is scheduled today, before any plan is published.
stages.actions: Logs in and reviews the Daily Dashboard for all published past and current-day services.
stages.pain: Open question: the SOW describes no OPS-specific review step distinct from the dashboard shared with GCSM.
stages.opportunity: Give Operations a dedicated day view, separate from the shared dashboard.

stages.name: Draft and publish the OPSKED
stages.goal: Produce a schedule the rest of the company can trust once it is published.
stages.actions: In draft: assigns vendors, Guest Ambassadors and service times, moves status from scheduled to in progress, then publishes.
stages.touchpoints: Daily OPSKED, draft and publish views
stages.pain: Billing fields OPS is expected to enter conflict with §1.9, which grants OPS no billing access at all.
stages.opportunity: Resolve the billing-permission contradiction before build, and add a lightweight vendor-conflict warning.
stages.emotion: Focused, mildly anxious — publishing locks the schedule

stages.name: Live execution monitoring
stages.goal: Catch delays, flight issues and status changes as they happen.
stages.actions: Monitors Live OPSKED service cards, works status filters and reminder timers, expands cards for detail.
stages.touchpoints: Live OPSKED dashboard, service cards, timers
stages.pain: No vendor availability check in MVP scope — a reassignment can silently double-book.
stages.opportunity: Add a real-time availability check as a flag, not a hard block.

stages.name: Issue and exception handling
stages.goal: Resolve disruptions before they reach the guest or the client.
stages.actions: Creates and progresses trouble tickets, tracks flight delays, combines and uncombines linked services, reassigns vendors and drivers.
stages.touchpoints: Trouble ticket module, reassignment UI, flight delay indicators
stages.pain: Auto-assignment rules are unresolved by the client, and ticket status-change notifications are missing from the consolidated table.
stages.opportunity: Finalise the auto-assignment rules, and add ticket-status alerts to the notification spec.

stages.name: Guest and vendor coordination
stages.goal: Keep vendor, driver and Guest Ambassador assignments conflict-free through the day.
stages.actions: Oversees check-in and checkout activity on service cards, confirms vendor task status.
stages.touchpoints: Live OPSKED guest check-in data, vendor assignments panel
stages.pain: Vendor has no defined permissions row, despite being granted ticket-transition rights in the narrative.
stages.opportunity: Define Vendor as a first-class role, or document OPS acting on a vendor’s behalf.

stages.name: Day-end closeout and rollover
stages.goal: Close the day with nothing silently dropped.
stages.actions: Reviews the automatic 23:59 export and confirms which services roll forward to tomorrow.
stages.touchpoints: Live OPSKED end-of-day export, next-day carryover
stages.pain: Offline and local sync has no documented conflict handling — the risk lands on low-connectivity field work.
stages.opportunity: Document offline conflict resolution before mobile access ships.
stages.emotion: Relieved but incomplete — unresolved items roll forward

solutions.name: Author the Operations journey to the depth the GCSM section already had
solutions.resolves: The critical role has no documented journey
solutions.detail: A dedicated OPS user flow, mapped from login through day-end rollover, with a node and edge reference table so it could be imported and worked on directly. It also forces the open question into the open: is OPS exactly GCSM permissions plus OPSKED ownership, or broader? That is the client’s answer to give, and it is now a question with a place to be answered rather than an absence.

solutions.name: Reconcile billing responsibility with billing access
solutions.detail: Two sections cannot both be right. Either the matrix grants OPS billing access to match the narrative, or OPS is restricted and the narrative and every downstream document are corrected. Presented as a decision with both costs stated, not a recommendation to accept.

solutions.name: A non-blocking overlap warning instead of a full availability calendar
solutions.resolves: A reassignment can silently double-book a vendor
solutions.detail: A full availability system was out of scope and would have stayed out. Flagging the same vendor on date- or time-overlapping services is a fraction of the cost, degrades safely, and puts the warning exactly where the mistake happens — at the moment of reassignment, with the person who can still undo it.

solutions.name: Define the conflict policy before offline ships
solutions.resolves: Offline support with no conflict rule
solutions.detail: Pick a rule — last write wins with an audit flag, or field-level merge — and specify it ahead of implementation. If neither can be settled in time, scope version one to read-only offline, which is honest about what it guarantees rather than silently losing a field edit.

title: Ledgerline
tagline: Month-end close cut from nine days to four for a 2,400-seat payables floor.
summary: A reconciliation console that treats matching as a judgement call, not a data-entry chore.
about: Kestrel Pay processed payables for mid-market manufacturers, but its reconciliation console had been grown, not designed — eleven years of finance-team requests bolted onto one table. Close took nine days, and three of those were analysts re-checking work the system had already done. The mandate was to raise auto-match rates without hiding the machine: controllers sign their name to the close, so every automated decision had to be inspectable, reversible, and defensible to an auditor who arrives four months later.

metrics.label: Month-end close
metrics.note: Down from nine, sustained across two quarters.

metrics.label: Auto-match rate
metrics.note: Up from 62% on identical transaction volume.

metrics.label: Fewer support tickets
metrics.note: Mostly the "why did it match this?" category, now answered in-product.

metrics.label: Per exception resolved
metrics.note: From 19 clicks to 7 on the median exception path.

research.intro: Six weeks of fieldwork across four customer finance teams, deliberately timed to land on their close days rather than a quiet Tuesday.

methods.name: Contextual inquiry
methods.detail: 11 sessions observed live during month-end close, two of them at 9pm.

methods.name: Support-ticket mining
methods.detail: 2,140 tickets from 18 months, coded into 9 recurring failure shapes.

methods.name: Analytics funnel review
methods.detail: Traced 40,000 exception resolutions to find where analysts abandoned mid-task.

methods.name: Artefact analysis
methods.detail: Collected the shadow spreadsheets 7 of 11 analysts kept beside the product.

research.insight: Analysts did not distrust the matching engine. They distrusted their ability to explain it to an auditor — so they redid its work by hand to have something to point at.

painPoints.label: The silent match
painPoints.detail: Auto-matched pairs left no trace of why they matched, so analysts re-derived the logic manually before signing off.

painPoints.label: Nineteen-click exceptions
painPoints.detail: Resolving one mismatch meant four screens, two of which existed only to confirm you meant it.

painPoints.label: Shadow spreadsheets
painPoints.detail: Seven of eleven analysts kept a private tracker because the product could not show close progress by owner.

painPoints.label: Audit panic
painPoints.detail: Reconstructing a decision from four months ago took an average of 25 minutes and a Slack thread.

competitors.name: Bandelier Close
competitors.verdict: Beautiful dashboards, but every automated decision is a black box you can only accept or reject.

competitors.name: Portico ERP module
competitors.verdict: Total auditability, buried under a 1990s tree navigation nobody opens twice.

competitors.name: Netter Reconcile
competitors.verdict: Fast rules engine aimed at bookkeepers — collapses on multi-entity intercompany volume.

competitiveAudit.whitespace: Nobody had made the match itself legible. Explaining a decision was treated as an audit feature bolted on later, never as the thing that lets a controller move quickly in the moment.

personas.name: Dana Okwuosa
personas.goal: Clear her queue by Thursday without leaving anything she cannot defend.
personas.frustration: Redoes work the system already did, because the system will not show its reasoning.
personas.quote: I trust it right up until someone asks me why. Then I start again from the bank file.

personas.name: Marcus Hale
personas.goal: Sign the close on time and survive the audit in April with no restatements.
personas.frustration: Cannot see whose queue is stuck until the day it makes him late.
personas.quote: I do not need it faster. I need to know at 4pm on day two whether we are going to be late.

journey.label: One month-end close, as it is actually lived

stages.name: Bank files land
stages.detail: Overnight imports drop 14,000 transactions into the queue.

stages.name: Triage the queue
stages.detail: Dana sorts by amount, not by risk, because risk is not a column.

stages.name: Re-check the auto-matches
stages.detail: Three days spent verifying decisions the engine already made correctly.

stages.name: Fight the exceptions
stages.detail: Nineteen clicks each, with two confirmation dialogs that teach nothing.

stages.name: Chase the stragglers
stages.detail: Marcus DMs four analysts to build a picture the product should have shown him.

stages.name: Sign the close
stages.detail: Nine days in, with a private spreadsheet as the real source of truth.

stages.name: April audit request
stages.detail: Reconstruct a single decision from memory, Slack, and luck.

solutions.name: Match Receipts
solutions.detail: Every automated pair carries a plain-language receipt — the rule that fired, the confidence, the two fields that clinched it — expandable inline and frozen into the audit record.

solutions.name: One-surface exceptions
solutions.detail: Exception resolution collapsed into a single split view with keyboard-first actions. Confirmation dialogs were replaced with a seven-second undo.

solutions.name: Close Board
solutions.detail: A live close view by owner, queue and risk band, so a controller can see a stall on day two instead of day eight.

solutions.name: Time-travel view
solutions.detail: Any transaction can be replayed at any past date — what the system knew, what it decided, who overrode it — in one link an auditor can be sent.

visualDesign.statement: Finance software earns trust by being boring in the right places. The language here is high-density and near-monochrome, with a single cool blue reserved exclusively for system-made decisions — so a controller scanning a screen can tell machine judgement from human judgement without reading a word. Numerals are tabular everywhere; nothing shifts as values update.

about: APTEN is a B2B marketplace that connects brands and manufacturers with third-party logistics providers through a structured RFP process. Instead of brands cold-calling warehouses, the platform handles the whole path — profile and volume data intake, algorithmic matching, long list to short list curation, a shared Data Room for evaluation, proposal comparison, and final award and onboarding.

research.intro: Desk research against genuine user-generated content and formal industry data, not assumption. Every claim below is traceable to a named source; where evidence was a single anecdote, it is labelled as one rather than generalised.

methods.name: Merchant forum mining
methods.detail: Shopify Community threads where brands describe 3PL billing and fulfilment failures in their own words.

methods.name: Formal industry survey
methods.detail: SCALA UK survey via Fleet News — 20% of UK companies report difficulties with their 3PL.

methods.name: Specialist consultancy analysis
methods.detail: Staci Americas and Fulfillrite on how 3PL RFPs are actually run, and the red flags brands miss.

methods.name: Verified review teardown
methods.detail: G2 reviews of Clutch and Freightos, read for distrust of the matching platforms themselves.

research.insight: Only 35% of customers agree with the 54% of 3PLs who rate their own performance as highly successful — a 19-point gap between what is claimed and what is experienced.
research.insightAttribution: SCALA UK industry survey, via Fleet News

painPoints.label: Rates move after you commit
painPoints.detail: Quoted pricing changes once inventory and money are already in. Documented cases moved $10 to $14.50 per order and $8 to $25 per label.
painPoints.evidence: Practical Ecommerce (Beardbrand); Shopify Community; Fulfillrite — Theme 1, high severity, three independent sources.

painPoints.label: Capability is indistinguishable from sales talk
painPoints.detail: Brands cannot separate real operational capacity from a team that says yes to everything, and there is no verified data to check it against before signing.
painPoints.evidence: SCALA/Fleet News UK survey; Fulfillrite red-flags analysis — Theme 2, high severity.

painPoints.label: The RFP is rushed and shallow
painPoints.detail: RFPs get launched reactively as a fix to an existing crisis, sent to too many vendors without pre-filtering, and without the operational data needed to price accurately.
painPoints.evidence: Staci Americas — Theme 3, recurring pattern across client engagements.

painPoints.label: The matching platforms are themselves distrusted
painPoints.detail: Reviewers report pay-for-placement undermining "verified" review claims, and platform fees that only surface at checkout.
painPoints.evidence: G2 reviews of Clutch.co and Freightos — Theme 6, formal review data.

matrix.caption: Where APTEN sits against the incumbents

competitors.name: Fulfill.com
competitors.verdict: Algorithmic matching plus human consultation, but fully form-gated with no RFP mechanism, no document exchange and a 3–5 day turnaround.

competitors.name: WarehousingAndFulfillment.com
competitors.verdict: Twenty years of curation and an 8% provider approval rate, wrapped in a basic UI with no proposal management and no transparency on how matching works.

competitors.name: Clutch.co
competitors.verdict: The most mature verified-review infrastructure in B2B services — undermined, per its own reviewers, by paid placement.

competitiveAudit.whitespace: Every incumbent stops at the introduction. None of them owns the evaluation — no shared document room, no structured proposal comparison, no contract record that holds after signing. That gap is exactly where the documented harm happens.

personas.name: The Fulfillment Decision-Maker
personas.quote: I can’t expect a fulfillment partner to care about my brand as much as I do.
goals: Find a 3PL that genuinely fits their volume and SKU profile without weeks of unstructured comparison.
Lock in pricing and SLA terms that will not change after signing.
See real operational performance data before committing, not just sales claims.
frustrations: A quoted rate changed materially after signing — real cases moved $10 to $14.50 per order.
Hard to tell real capability from a sales team that says yes to everything.
No pre-commitment visibility into performance, against a measured 19-point claim-versus-experience gap.
personas.note: They own the outcome when a 3PL relationship goes wrong — fielding the customer complaints and explaining the billing discrepancies to finance.

personas.name: The Business Development Lead
personas.quote: Generic pitches about warehouse locations and carrier relationships won’t win business anymore.
goals: Be matched with brands whose volume genuinely fits operational capacity, instead of chasing poor-fit prospects.
Differentiate on real operational outcomes rather than generic infrastructure claims.
Trust that platform fees are transparent and tied to genuinely qualified leads.
frustrations: The average 3PL sale needs six to eight touchpoints, but most reps give up after two or three.
Consultant and agency referral channels are underused across the industry.
Suspicion that competitors can buy visibility rather than earn it.
personas.note: Thinner evidence than persona one — the two trust frustrations are extrapolated from adjacent competitor review data, not confirmed 3PL-side complaints. Primary interviews would strengthen it.

journey.label: The brand user, from first search to signed contract

stages.name: Awareness
stages.goal: Recognise that the current fulfilment approach will not survive their order volume.
stages.actions: Searches online, asks peers for referrals — often already mid-crisis with the incumbent.
stages.touchpoints: Search results, industry blogs, word of mouth, competitor directories
stages.pain: RFPs get triggered reactively, in response to an active problem, never planned.
stages.opportunity: Speak directly to the reactive-search moment; help a rushed brand define real requirements before comparing anyone.

stages.name: Consideration
stages.goal: Decide whether APTEN is a trustworthy way to find a 3PL at all.
stages.actions: Weighs the value proposition against a manual search and the incumbent platforms.
stages.pain: Matching platforms carry documented distrust; a 19-point claim-versus-experience gap sits behind it.
stages.opportunity: Surface trust signals early — transparent deposit framing, evidence that matches are not pay-to-play.

stages.name: Onboarding & setup
stages.goal: Get business profile and operational data into the platform accurately.
stages.actions: Signs up, completes the business profile, uploads order history, builds the product catalog.
stages.touchpoints: Sign-up, onboarding wizard, Profile module, five-step Volume Profile
stages.pain: Gathering detailed operational history takes real time, but pricing accuracy later depends on it.
stages.opportunity: Reinforce graceful degradation — the "insufficient data" fallback belongs throughout onboarding, not only in the Data Room.

stages.name: Define requirements
stages.goal: Get matched with 3PLs that genuinely fit, without months of vetting.
stages.actions: Selects services, sets locations and budget, reviews the RFP dashboard and its matches.
stages.touchpoints: Define Requirements screen, RFP dashboard, Define Scope wizard, 3PL profiles
stages.pain: The matching logic is unspecified — the brand has no visibility into why a given 3PL surfaced.
stages.opportunity: Highest-leverage point to close the trust gap: even a lightweight "why this match" tied to Volume Profile data.

stages.name: Engagement & evaluation
stages.goal: Verify a shortlisted 3PL’s claims before committing money and inventory.
stages.actions: Invites 3PLs into the Data Room, reads documents, asks questions, compares proposals.
stages.touchpoints: Data Room, FAQ and Q&A, Ask a Question modal, proposal review
stages.pain: Quoted rates have moved after signing — $10 to $14.50 per order, $8 to $25 per label.
stages.opportunity: Resolve the open question in favour of server-side Cost Summary calculation — it closes a documented harm.

stages.name: Award & handoff
stages.goal: Formalise the partnership, confident the terms will hold.
stages.actions: Names a finalist, awards the winner, begins the Fulfilment Contract wizard.
stages.touchpoints: Award action, Fulfilment Contract wizard, Relationships kanban
stages.pain: This is exactly where documented cases show terms changing between agreement and execution.
stages.opportunity: Make the locked, platform-tracked contract record a headline value proposition, not a quiet backend detail.

solutions.name: Server-side Cost Summary and a locking contract wizard
solutions.detail: Cost is calculated server-side and the Fulfilment Contract wizard locks terms to match the Data Room proposal exactly. Post-signing changes require a logged, visible Change Request.

solutions.name: Mandatory, verified Performance Metrics
solutions.resolves: Capability is indistinguishable from sales talk
solutions.detail: A 3PL cannot receive RFP invitations until dispatch time, order accuracy and return processing are filled in and admin-verified, and they must be refreshed on a cadence so the data stays current.

solutions.name: A staged, pre-checked RFP flow
solutions.resolves: The RFP is rushed and shallow
solutions.detail: Define Scope, then Long List, then Short List — with a structured pre-RFP checklist that nudges order-history and volume data to completion before the brand can proceed.

solutions.name: Transparency as a first-class feature
solutions.resolves: The matching platforms are themselves distrusted
solutions.detail: A plain-language "how matching works" explainer, a "why this match" note tied to Volume Profile data on every suggestion, and the $100 deposit and 3PL billing model stated in full before signup.

title: Fair Weather
tagline: First notice of loss that stops turning a bad day into a bad month.
summary: A claims intake experience built around the twenty minutes after something goes wrong.
team: Me, 1 content designer, 1 researcher, 6 engineers, 2 claims SMEs
about: Merrowfield Mutual wrote home and small-commercial property policies across storm-exposed coastal states. Their first-notice-of-loss form was a faithful digital copy of a paper document: 62 fields, ordered by how the claims system stored data rather than how a person remembers an incident. Two thirds of policyholders abandoned it and phoned instead, at a call-handling cost the business had stopped questioning. The hard part was not the form. It was that claims intake happens on the worst day of someone’s year, often outdoors, often on a cracked phone, often while a contractor waits.

metrics.label: Digital FNOL completion
metrics.note: Up from 34% — the first release moved it more than the second.

metrics.label: Intake call volume
metrics.note: Measured over the first full storm season post-launch.

metrics.label: Median time to file
metrics.note: From 31 minutes, including photo capture.

metrics.label: Post-claim intake rating
metrics.note: From 3.1, on the same survey instrument.

research.intro: Research ran against real claims, not hypotheticals — including three ride-alongs with field adjusters during an active storm response.

methods.name: Diary study
methods.detail: 23 policyholders logged their first 72 hours after a loss, in their own words.

methods.name: Call-recording analysis
methods.detail: 180 intake calls transcribed and coded for the moment the caller gave up on the form.

methods.name: Field ride-alongs
methods.detail: Three days shadowing adjusters to see what intake data they actually reuse.

methods.name: Tree testing
methods.detail: Validated a loss-type taxonomy rewritten in claimant language, not policy language.

research.insight: People were not confused by the questions. They were afraid of them — every field read like a chance to say the wrong thing and lose the claim.

painPoints.label: The interrogation tone
painPoints.detail: Fields phrased in policy language read as accusatory, so claimants stalled and called a human for reassurance.

painPoints.label: All or nothing
painPoints.detail: No save state. A phone dying at field 40 meant starting over at field 1.

painPoints.label: Photos last
painPoints.detail: Image upload sat at the end, long after most people had already put the phone down.

painPoints.label: Silence after submit
painPoints.detail: A confirmation number and then nothing for four days — the single largest driver of follow-up calls.

competitors.name: Northgate Assurance
competitors.verdict: Slick mobile intake, but funnels every complex loss straight to a phone queue.

competitors.name: Halden Insurance app
competitors.verdict: Strong claim-status tracking bolted onto an intake flow that still asks for a policy number first.

competitors.name: Ravensworth Direct
competitors.verdict: Chat-led intake that feels human until it asks the same question three times.

competitiveAudit.whitespace: Every competitor optimised the filing. None designed the wait. The days between submitting and hearing back were unowned territory, and that is exactly where trust was being lost.

personas.name: Rosa Villalobos
personas.goal: Get the roof tarped and understand whether she is covered before the next storm.
personas.frustration: Cannot tell which questions are required and which will be held against her.
personas.quote: I kept re-reading it. I did not want to write the wrong thing and have that be the reason they said no.

personas.name: Terrence Boyd
personas.goal: Arrive at a property already knowing what he is looking at.
personas.frustration: Half his assignments arrive with a photo of a wet ceiling and no address detail worth using.
personas.quote: Give me four good photos and the date it started. I can do the rest from the truck.

journey.label: From the moment of loss to first adjuster contact

stages.name: It happens
stages.detail: Water through the ceiling at 6am; the priority is stopping it, not filing anything.

stages.name: Stabilise
stages.detail: Buckets, towels, a call to a roofer who asks for a claim number she does not have.

stages.name: Find the policy
stages.detail: Digging for a policy number the app should never have asked her for.

stages.name: Start the form
stages.detail: Sixty-two fields in policy language, no sense of how long this will take.

stages.name: Abandon and call
stages.detail: Twelve minutes on hold to have a person confirm she is not making it worse.

stages.name: The silence
stages.detail: Four days with a confirmation number and no visible progress.

stages.name: Adjuster calls
stages.detail: Finally a human with context — the first genuinely reassuring moment.

solutions.name: Ask like a person
solutions.detail: Every question rewritten with a content designer into claimant language, with a one-line "why we ask" beneath anything that sounds legally loaded.

solutions.name: Resumable by default
solutions.detail: Intake saves on every field change and can be resumed from a text-message link — no account, no password, no re-entry.

solutions.name: Photos first
solutions.detail: Capture opens the flow while the claimant is still standing in front of the damage, with four guided shots adjusters said they actually reuse.

solutions.name: The visible wait
solutions.detail: A claim timeline showing what has happened, what is next, and who owns it — plus a named adjuster and an honest date range, not a promise.

visualDesign.statement: This one had to feel calm before it felt clever. Generous type sizes for outdoor phone use in bad light, one question per screen, and a soft violet reserved for anything the insurer commits to — dates, ownership, next steps — so a claimant scanning in a panic can find the promises. No progress percentages, which tested as pressure; a plain step count instead.

title: Shopfloor Signal
tagline: Gave line supervisors a downtime story they could act on before the shift ended.
summary: Downtime capture designed for gloved hands, loud rooms, and ninety free seconds.
about: Vantera ran fourteen plants on an OEE platform that produced immaculate weekly reports nobody used to change anything. Downtime reasons were logged by supervisors from memory at end of shift, which meant the data was roughly right and completely useless — everything landed in a bucket called "Other, minor stop". The mandate was to make capture fast enough to happen at the machine, in the moment, by someone wearing gloves. The constraint that shaped everything: a supervisor has about ninety uninterrupted seconds, and the room is too loud to think in.

metrics.label: Stops logged within 5 min
metrics.note: Up from 11% logged same-shift.

metrics.label: OEE lift on pilot lines
metrics.note: Sustained over two quarters at three plants.

metrics.label: "Other" reason codes
metrics.note: The bucket that used to swallow a third of all downtime.

metrics.label: Median time to log a stop
metrics.note: Two taps and a reason, gloves on.

research.intro: Five days on three shop floors across two plants, including two night shifts, plus a teardown of eighteen months of reason-code data.

methods.name: Shadowing
methods.detail: 11 supervisors observed across day, swing and night shifts.

methods.name: Reason-code forensics
methods.detail: Traced 34,000 logged stops to find where the taxonomy collapsed into "Other".

methods.name: Glove testing
methods.detail: Tap-target trials with three glove types on the actual wall-mounted panels.

methods.name: Shift-handover interviews
methods.detail: What actually gets passed on verbally, and why it never reaches the system.

research.insight: Supervisors were not skipping the log because it was long. They were skipping it because it asked for a cause at the exact moment they were still fixing the effect.

painPoints.label: Cause before cure
painPoints.detail: The system demanded a root cause while the line was still down and hands were still busy.

painPoints.label: Taxonomy by committee
painPoints.detail: 84 reason codes written by corporate engineering, none in the words the floor actually uses.

painPoints.label: Gloves versus targets
painPoints.detail: Touch targets sized for a mouse, on a panel only ever used with gloves on.

painPoints.label: Reports nobody reads
painPoints.detail: Weekly PDFs arriving Monday about a problem that was solved or forgotten on Wednesday.

competitors.name: Aldergate MES
competitors.verdict: Deep scheduling engine, an interface that assumes a seated operator with a keyboard.

competitors.name: Provec OEE
competitors.verdict: Genuinely good dashboards for plant managers; nothing at all for the person at the machine.

competitors.name: Kirinmark Tablet
competitors.verdict: Right hardware instincts, wrong data model — every stop needs a cause before it can be saved.

competitiveAudit.whitespace: Everyone built for the plant manager reading yesterday. Nobody built for the supervisor standing at a stopped line right now — which is the only moment the data is cheap to collect and worth anything.

personas.name: Ivan Prokopenko
personas.goal: Get the line running and hand over a shift that does not create work for the next one.
personas.frustration: Logging a stop properly costs him the same ninety seconds he needs to fix it.
personas.quote: I will tell you exactly what happened. Just not while it is still happening.

personas.name: Priya Raghunathan
personas.goal: Find the two recurring stops costing her the most, and prove it to corporate.
personas.frustration: A third of her downtime data says "Other", which is the same as no data.
personas.quote: I can defend a number. I cannot defend a bucket labelled Other.

journey.label: A single unplanned stop, from klaxon to root cause

stages.name: Line stops
stages.detail: Klaxon, andon light, and three people converging on the same machine.

stages.name: Triage
stages.detail: Ivan diagnoses by ear before he touches a panel.

stages.name: Fix
stages.detail: Eleven minutes, gloves on, both hands occupied.

stages.name: Restart
stages.detail: Line back up; the system now wants a root cause from a menu of 84.

stages.name: Defer the log
stages.detail: Tap "Other, minor stop" and promise himself he will fix it later.

stages.name: Shift handover
stages.detail: Real story told verbally to the next supervisor, recorded nowhere.

stages.name: Monday report
stages.detail: Priya reads a chart in which a third of the truth is missing.

solutions.name: Two-tap stop
solutions.detail: Logging splits in half: mark the stop in two gloved taps now, attach the cause from a phone during handover. Capture stops competing with repair.

solutions.name: Floor vocabulary
solutions.detail: 84 codes rewritten into 19, in the words supervisors used while being shadowed, with per-line ordering by actual frequency.

solutions.name: Glove-first panel
solutions.detail: Minimum 72px targets, high-contrast at a two-metre glance, and no interaction that needs precision or a second hand.

solutions.name: The shift card
solutions.detail: One card at handover: the three stops that cost this shift the most, and whether they are getting worse. It replaced the Monday PDF entirely.

visualDesign.statement: Designed to be read at two metres, in a room lit by sodium lamps, by someone who is not going to lean in. Everything is oversized, high-contrast and stripped of decoration; amber carries state and only state, so a glance across the floor tells you whether a line is fine without reading a single label. Nothing animates on the panel — motion on a shop floor means a machine is moving, and the interface has no business borrowing that signal.

title: Dwell
tagline: Eleven distribution centres, 41% less driver detention, one honest appointment.
summary: Dock scheduling rebuilt around the only number carriers actually care about.
about: Northbay ran eleven distribution centres where dock appointments were booked in a portal, confirmed by email, and then ignored by everyone. Drivers waited an average of 94 minutes past their slot; carriers billed detention; site managers blamed carriers; carriers blamed sites. The mandate was to cut detention spend. The difficulty was political rather than technical — an accurate appointment makes a site look bad, so every honest signal in the system had been quietly rounded off by the people it embarrassed.

metrics.label: Driver detention hours
metrics.note: Across eleven sites, first two quarters.

metrics.label: Average dwell
metrics.note: From 94 minutes over slot down to 55.

metrics.label: Annualised detention avoided
metrics.note: Finance-validated, net of the two sites that regressed.

metrics.label: Appointments kept
metrics.note: Up from 51% — measured against the slot, not the day.

research.intro: Two weeks split between the guard shack and the yard office, plus 30 carrier dispatchers interviewed by phone because that is the only way they ever talk to anyone.

methods.name: Yard observation
methods.detail: 4 sites, 6am–2pm, counting where the 94 minutes actually went.

methods.name: Driver intercepts
methods.detail: 38 short interviews in the cab, in the queue, while waiting.

methods.name: Dispatcher interviews
methods.detail: 30 carrier-side conversations about how they really plan a route.

methods.name: Telematics reconciliation
methods.detail: Compared GPS arrival times against booked slots and logged check-ins.

research.insight: The appointment was never the problem. Every party had learned to treat it as fiction, so each one padded their own estimate — and the padding was the delay.

painPoints.label: The fiction slot
painPoints.detail: Appointment times were aspirational, so carriers padded arrivals and sites padded capacity, compounding both.

painPoints.label: Check-in by clipboard
painPoints.detail: Arrival was recorded when a guard walked out, not when the truck arrived — the gap was pure unrecorded dwell.

painPoints.label: No shared clock
painPoints.detail: Site, carrier and driver each had a different arrival timestamp, and every detention dispute became forensics.

painPoints.label: Rebooking means phoning
painPoints.detail: A delayed driver could not move a slot without a call nobody had time to take.

competitors.name: Tidewater Dock
competitors.verdict: Best-in-class booking calendar; treats what happens after the truck arrives as somebody else’s software.

competitors.name: Grantham Yard OS
competitors.verdict: Powerful yard-move orchestration for the site, nothing at all in the driver’s hand.

competitors.name: Loadway Portal
competitors.verdict: Carrier-friendly and quick to book, but the site can silently override any slot without telling anyone.

competitiveAudit.whitespace: Every product served one side of the gate. None gave the site, the carrier and the driver the same timestamp — and detention disputes are, in the end, an argument about whose clock is real.

personas.name: Curtis Nwosu
personas.goal: Two more stops today, which means knowing now whether he is waiting an hour.
personas.frustration: No way to tell a late slot from a moving one until he is already parked.
personas.quote: Tell me it is going to be ninety minutes and I will go eat. Do not tell me twenty and mean ninety.

personas.name: Lorena Batiste
personas.goal: Keep doors flowing without a queue that spills onto the county road.
personas.frustration: Half her arrivals are unannounced early, and the system rewards her for looking punctual, not being punctual.
personas.quote: I can absorb a late truck. What I cannot absorb is six early ones nobody warned me about.

journey.label: One inbound load, gate to gate

stages.name: Book the slot
stages.detail: Dispatcher picks a time everyone privately treats as approximate.

stages.name: Roll in
stages.detail: Curtis pads by 45 minutes because being late is worse than waiting.

stages.name: Arrive early
stages.detail: Parks on the shoulder; nothing in the system knows he is there.

stages.name: Check in
stages.detail: Clipboard at the shack, timestamp written when the guard gets to him.

stages.name: Wait
stages.detail: Ninety-four minutes with no visibility and no way to leave.

stages.name: Door assignment
stages.detail: A yard hostler waves him in; no notice, no ETA before it happens.

stages.name: Unload and out
stages.detail: Fast once it starts — the dock was never the bottleneck.

stages.name: Detention dispute
stages.detail: Three weeks later, two clocks disagree and someone eats the cost.

solutions.name: The honest slot
solutions.detail: Appointments show a live confidence band instead of a single time, recalculated from real door throughput. Sites stopped being punished for accuracy, so accuracy appeared.

solutions.name: Geofence check-in
solutions.detail: Arrival is stamped when the truck crosses the geofence, not when a guard notices. The clipboard became a fallback rather than the system of record.

solutions.name: One clock, three views
solutions.detail: Driver, site and carrier read the same timeline off the same events — the detention conversation moved from forensics to arithmetic.

solutions.name: Self-serve reslot
solutions.detail: A running-late driver can shift their own slot from a text link if capacity allows, and the site sees it before the truck does.

visualDesign.statement: Three audiences, one system, wildly different conditions — a phone in bright sun with one thumb, a yard-office monitor, a dispatcher’s third browser tab. The language leans on a single green used only for confirmed, shared facts; anything estimated stays outlined and uncoloured. That one rule does most of the work: on any screen, filled means agreed, and agreed is the only thing anyone can bill against.
